## How to read this lecture

There is one more thing from the Doppler shift that we have not yet explored,
and it turns out to be the thing that lets us recognize a black hole on sight.

[In lecture 3](../special-relativity/index.qmd) we worked out what relative
motion does to the *wavelength* of light. That is the half of the Doppler
effect everybody meets first, and it is the half that does the work in most of
astronomy: a line shifts, you read off a velocity, you go home. This lecture is
about the other half. The same motion, by the same factor, also changes how
*bright* the source looks — and it changes brightness far more violently than
it changes color. That asymmetry is written all over the two black holes we
have actually photographed.

Before we can get there we need one piece of background that this course has so
far assumed rather than stated: what light *is*, and how its wavelength, its
frequency and its energy are related. That is the first section, and it is
short.

The lecture then has three payoffs, in increasing order of spectacle. The first
is GPS, which is relativity doing an ordinary job in your pocket. The second is
Doppler beaming, which is the new physics. The third is a pair of photographs.

* ESO,

**If you want to go further**, the black hole in *Interstellar* was rendered by
a visual-effects team working with Kip Thorne, and their code was accurate
enough that it became
[a published paper](https://doi.org/10.1088/0264-9381/32/6/065001)

with its colors shifted, then with its brightness shifted too. Optional.

## Light is a wave

Light is a wave, and like any wave it has a wavelength $\lambda$ and a
frequency $\nu$. For light in a vacuum the two are locked together by the one
speed that never changes:

$$
c = \lambda\nu .
$$ {#eq-cln}

Nothing in @eq-cln is new physics — it is the definition of a wave speed,
applied to the one wave whose speed [we already know is the same for
everybody](../special-relativity/index.qmd). What it means in practice is that
wavelength and frequency are not two independent facts about a photon. Give one
and you have given the other. Long wavelength means low frequency; short
wavelength means high.

Light is also a particle, and this is where the two descriptions meet. A single
photon carries an energy set entirely by its frequency:

$$
E = h\nu ,
$$ {#eq-ehn}

where $h = 6.6262 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{erg\,s}$ is Planck's constant. Put
@eq-cln and @eq-ehn together and the chain is complete: **short wavelength =
high frequency = energetic photon**. That single chain is why a gamma ray will
break a chemical bond and a radio photon will not, and it is the reason
astronomers describe the same object by wavelength in one breath and by energy
in the next. They are the same statement.

The whole range of possibilities is the **electromagnetic spectrum**, and
visible light is a startlingly thin slice of it — roughly 4000 to 7000
angstroms, less than a factor of two in wavelength, against the twenty-odd
factors of ten the spectrum covers in total. Everything else in it is invisible
to your eye and perfectly ordinary to a telescope. Both of the black hole
images at the end of this lecture were taken at a wavelength of 1.3
millimeters, which is to say in the radio.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why a black hole is imaged in the radio and not in visible light"}
Two reasons, and they pull in the same direction.

The first is that the gas near the black hole is not trying to emit visible
light. It is hot, magnetized plasma radiating by synchrotron emission, and it
is brightest in the radio and millimeter bands. Pointing an optical telescope
at it would be looking where the light is not.

The second is that the sightline is filthy. The center of our Galaxy sits
behind tens of magnitudes of dust extinction — visible light from Sgr A\* does
not reach us at all. Millimeter waves pass through dust essentially unimpeded,
which is why the radio is the only band in which the picture can be taken.
:::

Both relations are worth using once before they are needed in anger. The
H$\alpha$ line of hydrogen has a rest wavelength of $6563\ \text{Å}$, and
here are its frequency and the energy of one of its photons, carried
through with the units attached at every step.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example (together): the energy of an H$\\alpha$ photon"}
**Frequency first.** Rearranging @eq-cln gives $\nu = c/\lambda$. The speed
of light is in $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$ and the wavelength is in angstroms, so
they have to be brought into the same units before they can be divided.
Write the equivalence as a fraction, arranged so that the angstroms cancel:

$$
\lambda = 6563\ \text{Å} \times
          \frac{10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \text{Å}}
        = 6.563 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm}
$$

Now the division is meaningful:

$$
\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda}
    = \frac{2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}}
           {6.563 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm}}
$$

The centimeters cancel and leave $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. *Do the units make
sense?* A frequency is a number of oscillations per second, which is exactly
an inverse second, so yes.

$$
\nu = 4.568 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 4.568 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}
$$

**Then the energy**, from @eq-ehn:

$$
E = h\nu = \left(6.6262 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{erg\,s}\right)
           \left(4.568 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\right)
$$

The seconds cancel against the inverse seconds and leave ergs.
*Do the units make sense?* An erg is a unit of energy and a photon energy is
an energy, so yes.

$$
E = 3.027 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{erg}
$$

**Finally in electron volts**, using the conversion from your constants
sheet, again as a fraction arranged so that the ergs cancel:

$$
E = 3.027 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{erg} \times
    \frac{6.242 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{eV}}{1\ \mathrm{erg}}
  = 1.89\ \mathrm{eV}
$$

A couple of electron volts is the characteristic energy of visible light,
and it is no coincidence that it is also the characteristic energy of a
chemical bond. That is why your eye works.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-light}

1. Repeat that calculation for an X-ray photon of wavelength
   $1\ \text{Å}$. How
   many times more energetic is it than the H$\alpha$ photon, and could you
   have predicted that ratio without doing either calculation?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answers"}
   $\nu = 3.00 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{Hz}$,
   $E = 1.99 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{erg} = 1.24 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{eV}$,
   which is $6563$ times the H$\alpha$ energy.

   Yes. Energy is proportional to frequency and frequency is inversely
   proportional to wavelength, so the energy ratio is just the *inverse* of the
   wavelength ratio: $6563/1 = 6563$. The two calculations were never
   independent.
   :::

2. A photon is emitted, travels across the Galaxy, and is absorbed. Its
   wavelength when it arrives is longer than when it left. Give two physically
   different reasons that could have happened, both of which you have already
   met in this course.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   One of them is in lecture 3 and needs the source to be *moving*. The other
   is in lecture 5 and needs the source to be sitting *deeper in a
   gravitational well* than you are — the photon loses energy climbing out,
   with nothing moving at all.
   :::
:::

## The Doppler shift, recalled

We are about to lean hard on the relativistic Doppler shift, so it is worth
having it in front of you rather than two lectures back. [The full derivation
is in lecture 3](../special-relativity/#relativistic-doppler-shift-of-light)
and nothing here supersedes it.

A source emitting at wavelength $\lambda$ and moving with **radial velocity**
$v_r$ relative to you is observed at

$$
\lambda^{\prime} = \lambda \left(1 + \frac{v_r}{c}\right)\gamma ,
$$ {#eq-doppler}

with the sign convention that $v_r > 0$ means the source is moving *away* and
$v_r < 0$ means it is coming *toward* you, and with
$\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$ as always. Two separate effects are stacked
inside @eq-doppler and it pays to keep them apart:

* the factor $(1 + v_r/c)$ is the **ordinary Doppler effect** — the source
  chases its own wavefronts, crowding them on approach and stretching them on
  recession. It depends on the direction of motion and it changes sign.
* the factor $\gamma$ is **time dilation** — the emitter's clock runs slow, so
  the whole wave train is spread over more of your time. It does not care about
  direction at all, because it depends on $v^2$.

The second one is the piece that only relativity supplies, and it is the reason
the classical formula served astronomy perfectly well for a century: $\gamma$
departs from 1 at order $\beta^2$, while the ordinary term departs from 1 at
order $\beta$. At the speeds of stars and galaxies the difference is invisible.
Near a black hole it is not.

Astronomers usually quote the shift as a **redshift**,

$$
z \equiv \frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda} - 1 ,
$$ {#eq-z}

which is a ratio of two lengths and therefore a pure number, defined so that
$z = 0$ means no shift at all.

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch: the same symbol, three different jobs"}
The letter $z$ is doing heavy duty in astronomy. Here it is a *kinematic*
redshift caused by motion. In [lecture
5](../strong-gravity/#gravitational-redshift) the identical quantity was
produced by climbing out of a gravitational well, with no motion at all. In
cosmology it is produced by the expansion of space itself.

The number is measured the same way in all three cases — you compare an
observed wavelength to a known rest wavelength — and it is the *interpretation*
that differs. A measured $z$ does not come with a label saying which mechanism
made it. Working out which one you are looking at is a large part of the job.
:::

## GPS

Here is a piece of relativity you have been carrying in your pocket.

A GPS satellite does one thing: it broadcasts, continuously, the time on its
own atomic clock together with a statement of where it is. Your phone listens
to several satellites at once, notes that the timestamps arriving from each are
slightly stale, converts each staleness into a distance by multiplying by $c$,
and finds the one point in space consistent with all of them. The entire system
is a distance measurement dressed up as a clock reading, and its accuracy is
therefore an accuracy in timekeeping.

The exchange rate is brutal and easy to remember: light travels almost exactly
one foot in one nanosecond. The satellite clocks are good to something like
25 nanoseconds, which is 7.5 meters of position, and that is where the "accurate
to within about ten meters" figure on the back of the box comes from.

Now put the satellites in orbit and both of the effects in this course turn up
at once, pulling in opposite directions.

**Special relativity slows the satellite clocks down.** They orbit at a radius
of about $26{,}600\ \mathrm{km}$ from the center of the Earth, which works out
to $3.87\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. That is a $\beta$ of $1.3 \times 10^{-5}$,
utterly negligible for anything else you would ever do with it, and
$\gamma - 1 \approx \beta^2/2 = 8.3 \times 10^{-11}$. Over a day that
accumulates to

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{SR}} \approx -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta^2 \times 86{,}400\ \mathrm{s}
                        = -7.2\ \mathrm{\mu s\ per\ day} ,
$$ {#eq-gpssr}

with the minus sign meaning the moving clock falls behind.

**General relativity speeds them up.** [Lecture 5](../strong-gravity/#gravitational-time-dilation)
gave the rate of a clock at radius $r$ as $\sqrt{1 - r_S/r}$ times the rate far
away. Deep in a well the clock is slow — and the satellite is *less* deep than
you are. Expanding the square root for the Earth's very weak field, the
difference between the two clocks comes out to

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{GR}} \approx \frac{GM_{\oplus}}{c^{2}}
   \left(\frac{1}{R_{\oplus}} - \frac{1}{a}\right) \times 86{,}400\ \mathrm{s}
   = +45.7\ \mathrm{\mu s\ per\ day} ,
$$ {#eq-gpsgr}

with the plus sign meaning the satellite clock runs ahead of yours.

The two do not cancel. They do not even come close:

$$
-7.2 + 45.7 = +38.5\ \mathrm{\mu s\ per\ day} .
$$

Left uncorrected, that is a timing error of $38.5\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ after one
day, and multiplying by $c$ turns it into **11.5 kilometers of position error,
accumulating every day.** The system would be useless within about two minutes
of being switched on, and unusable by lunchtime.

It is worth being precise about what this does and does not prove. It is not a
test of relativity — the corrections were designed in from the start, not
discovered afterward by a confused engineer. What it is, is a demonstration
that the two effects are *quantitatively* right at the part-in-$10^{10}$ level,
every day, in a system that a billion people would notice breaking.

::: {.callout-note title="Where the other half of this went"}
[Lecture 3's fifth Doppler exercise](../special-relativity/#sec-exercises-doppler)
asked you to work out the special-relativistic half of this, and then told you
the real correction had the opposite sign, was several times larger, and was
the subject of an upcoming lecture. This is that.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-gps}

1. Work out the general-relativistic drift for yourself. Take
   $GM_{\oplus}/c^{2} = 0.443\ \mathrm{cm}$, the Earth's radius as
   $6.37 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and the orbit radius as
   $2.66 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and confirm the $+45.7\ \mathrm{\mu s}$
   per day in @eq-gpsgr.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   Substitute into @eq-gpsgr with the units attached and do no arithmetic yet:

   $$
   \frac{\Delta t_{\mathrm{GR}}}{\Delta t}
     = 0.443\ \mathrm{cm} \left(
        \frac{1}{6.37 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}}
      - \frac{1}{2.66 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{cm}} \right)
   $$

   The bracket has units of inverse centimeters and the prefactor has units of
   centimeters, so they cancel and the rate difference is a pure number.
   *Do the units make sense?* It is a ratio of two clock rates, so it must be
   dimensionless — and it is.

   $$
   \frac{\Delta t_{\mathrm{GR}}}{\Delta t}
     = 0.443\left(1.570 \times 10^{-9} - 3.759 \times 10^{-10}\right)
     = 5.29 \times 10^{-10}
   $$

   Over one day:

   $$
   \Delta t_{\mathrm{GR}} = 5.29 \times 10^{-10} \times 86{,}400\ \mathrm{s}
     = 4.57 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s} = 45.7\ \mathrm{\mu s}
   $$

   Note which term dominates. The satellite is four times farther from the
   center of the Earth than you are, so its own $1/a$ contributes only a
   quarter as much as your $1/R_{\oplus}$ — most of the effect is *your* clock
   being slow, not the satellite's being fast.
   :::

2. A colleague proposes that since one effect is negative and the other
   positive, an orbit could be chosen at which they cancel exactly and no
   relativistic correction would be needed at all. Is there such an orbit? If
   so, say roughly where it is; if not, say why not.

:::

## Doppler beaming

Everything so far has been about *color*. A source moving toward you looks
bluer and a source moving away looks redder, by the factor in @eq-doppler. That
is the half of the Doppler effect that lecture 3 covered and that almost every
introduction stops at.

It is not the whole story, and the missing half is larger.

Define the **Doppler factor** as the amount by which the observed frequency is
boosted — the reciprocal of the wavelength stretch in @eq-doppler:

$$
\mathcal{D} \equiv \frac{\lambda}{\lambda^{\prime}} = \frac{\nu^{\prime}}{\nu}
  = \frac{1}{\left(1 + v_r/c\right)\gamma} .
$$ {#eq-dfactor}

Approach gives $\mathcal{D} > 1$ and recession gives $\mathcal{D} < 1$. Now ask
not what color the source appears, but how *bright*. Three separate things
happen, and every one of them scales with the same $\mathcal{D}$.

**One: each photon arrives with more energy.** From @eq-ehn the energy of a
photon is $h\nu$, and the frequency has been multiplied by $\mathcal{D}$. So
has the energy. That is one factor of $\mathcal{D}$.

**Two: the photons arrive more often.** The same crowding of wavefronts that
shortened the wavelength also compresses the interval between one photon and
the next, so a given number of them is delivered in less of your time. That is
a second factor of $\mathcal{D}$.

**Three: the light is swept forward into a narrower cone.** A source moving
toward you does not radiate the same amount in every direction as it would at
rest; its emission is thrown forward, like the headlights of a car. More of
what it emits lands on you and less goes elsewhere. That concentration turns
out to be worth two more factors of $\mathcal{D}$.

Multiply the three together:

$$
F \propto \mathcal{D}^{4} .
$$ {#eq-beaming}

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="How the third factor comes out to exactly two powers of the Doppler factor"}
The forward sweeping is **relativistic aberration**: the direction a photon
travels is not the same in the source's frame and in yours, and a moving source
therefore sees its own isotropic emission arrive at you concentrated.

The clean route is not to track the cone at all, but to use a conserved
quantity. The combination $I_\nu/\nu^3$ — specific intensity divided by the
cube of the frequency — is the same in every frame; this is a consequence of
Liouville's theorem, which says that photons do not bunch up or thin out in
phase space just because you changed frames. So

$$
\frac{I_{\nu^{\prime}}^{\prime}}{\nu^{\prime 3}} = \frac{I_\nu}{\nu^3}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
I_{\nu^{\prime}}^{\prime} = \mathcal{D}^{3} I_\nu ,
$$

and integrating over all frequencies picks up one more factor of
$\mathcal{D}$, giving @eq-beaming. The three-and-one split there is a different
bookkeeping of the same four powers as the argument above; both are correct and
the invariant is the shorter road.

**This box is for the ones who are going further.** Specific intensity is not
something ASTRO 206 uses, and none of it will be asked of you here. But if you
carry on into astrophysics you will meet $I_\nu$ in your first radiative
transfer course and you will meet this invariant with it, and it is worth
having seen once that it is the thing standing behind a picture you have
already looked at. The standard treatment is Rybicki and Lightman
[-@rybicki1979], in the chapter on relativistic covariance — it is the book
essentially every graduate program uses for this, and it is where to go if you
want the derivation done properly rather than gestured at.

The reason it is in these notes at all is that @eq-beaming would otherwise be a
fact handed down from nowhere, and that it is the same $\nu^3$ that Thorne's
team used to render *Interstellar* [@james2015].
:::

Now put a disk around a black hole and look at it edge-on-ish. The gas on one
side of the ring is coming toward you, the gas on the other side is going away,
and both are moving at the same speed. Write the inclination as $i$, with
$i = 0$ face-on and $i = 90^{\circ}$ edge-on, so that the radial velocity of
the approaching side is $-\beta c \sin i$ and of the receding side is
$+\beta c \sin i$. Put those into @eq-dfactor, take the ratio, and the factors
of $\gamma$ cancel — they are the same on both sides, because $\gamma$ does not
care about direction:

$$
\frac{F_{\mathrm{app}}}{F_{\mathrm{rec}}}
  = \left(\frac{1 + \beta\sin i}{1 - \beta\sin i}\right)^{4} .
$$ {#eq-ratio}

Compare that with the wavelength ratio between the same two sides, which is the
bracket without the exponent. The result is worth stating on its own line,
because it is the whole lesson of this lecture:

$$
\frac{F_{\mathrm{app}}}{F_{\mathrm{rec}}}
  = \left(\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{app}}}\right)^{4} .
$$ {#eq-fourthpower}

**The brightness ratio is the fourth power of the color ratio.** A shift in
color that you would have to measure with a spectrograph to notice is a shift
in brightness that is obvious in a photograph.

Some numbers, for a disk seen at $i = 60^{\circ}$:

| $\beta$ | color ratio | brightness ratio |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 1.19 | 2.0 |
| 0.2 | 1.42 | 4.1 |
| 0.3 | 1.70 | 8.4 |
| 0.5 | 2.53 | 40.8 |

At a tenth of the speed of light the color shift is a 19% effect — real, but
you would need an instrument. The brightness has already doubled.

The last row is not a hypothetical. [The innermost stable circular orbit](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd)
around a non-spinning black hole sits at $3\,r_S$, and gas there orbits at
**exactly half the speed of light**, for a black hole of any mass whatsoever —
the same cancellation that ran through all of lecture 5. So the inner disk of a
black hole is a place where one side is genuinely forty times brighter than the
other.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what happens to the part of the ring moving straight across your line of sight"}
At the top and bottom of the ring the motion is transverse: $v_r = 0$, so the
ordinary Doppler term is exactly 1 and there is no crowding of wavefronts at
all. Classically, nothing should happen there.

Relativistically, $\mathcal{D} = 1/\gamma$, which is less than one. That gas is
**redshifted and dimmed even though it is neither approaching nor receding** —
purely because its clock is running slow. At $\beta = 0.5$ the effect is not
subtle: the light is reddened by 15%, and @eq-beaming dims it to
$1/\gamma^4 = 56\%$ of what it would be at rest.

So a relativistic disk is not simply bright on one side and faint on the other.
It is bright on one side and faint everywhere else.
:::

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-beaming}

1. A disk is seen at $i = 30^{\circ}$ and its gas orbits at $\beta = 0.4$.
   Calculate the ratio of wavelengths between the approaching and receding
   sides, and the ratio of brightnesses.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answers"}
   $\beta\sin i = 0.200$, so the color ratio is $1.200/0.800 = 1.50$ and the
   brightness ratio is $1.50^{4} = 5.06$.
   :::

2. Show that the factors of $\gamma$ cancel when @eq-ratio is formed, and say
   in one sentence why that had to happen without doing any algebra.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Ask what $\gamma$ depends on, and whether the two sides of the ring differ
   in that quantity.
   :::

3. Steve and Alex are looking at the same accretion disk. Steve measures a
   color ratio of 1.3 between the two sides. Alex, without measuring any
   wavelengths at all, reports a brightness ratio. What number should Alex get,
   and what does that tell you about which of the two measurements is easier?

4. A disk is seen exactly face-on. Show from @eq-ratio that there is no
   beaming asymmetry at all, and then say — using the previous Resolution
   callout — whether that means relativity has no visible effect on the disk's
   appearance.

5. The approaching side of a disk is measured to be 50 times brighter than the
   receding side. What is $\beta\sin i$? Can you determine $\beta$ from this
   measurement alone?
:::

## What a black hole looks like

A black hole emits nothing. Everything in a picture of one is light from gas
that has not fallen in yet, bent on its way out. So the question "what does a
black hole look like" is really two questions — where is the gas, and what does
the geometry do to its light on the way to us — and we now have the pieces for
both.

side is conspicuously brighter than its right, labeled Doppler beaming: light
from gas moving toward the viewer is brighter, and from gas moving away,
fainter. The disk does not pass behind the black hole as it would in flat
space; instead its far side is bent up and over the top into an arch, labeled
image of the disk's far side, and its underside is bent up beneath into a
second arch, labeled image of the disk's underside. A thin bright circle just
inside those arches is labeled photon ring, made of light that orbited the
black hole two or more times before escaping. The dark region it encloses is
labeled black hole shadow, roughly twice the size of the event horizon."}

<!-- NASA is public domain, so the credit is requested rather than legally
     required -- but it is given anyway, and in the caption rather than in a
     comment, because that is where lecture 5 puts credits and because a
     reader cannot see an HTML comment. Source file BH_labeled.jpg,
     3851x2166, resized to 1600x900 at quality 86 (150 KB). -->

Work through @fig-anatomy one feature at a time.

**The disk is brighter on one side.** That is @eq-ratio, and it is the only
feature in the picture you could have predicted before this lecture. The gas is
orbiting; one side comes toward you and one side goes away; the fourth power
does the rest.

**The far side of the disk is not hidden.** In flat space a disk seen nearly
edge-on would disappear behind the central object. Here the light from the far
side is bent up and over the top, so the disk appears to rise into an arch
above the hole. There is a second arch below, which is the *underside* of the
far side, lensed the other way. Neither is a separate structure. You are seeing
the same disk from three directions at once.

**There is a thin bright circle just outside the darkness.** That is the
**photon ring**, and lecture 5 already named the reason for it: at $1.5\,r_S$
there is a [photon sphere](../strong-gravity/#black-holes-from-the-theory-this-time)
where light can orbit. Rays that wind around the hole two, three, or more times
before escaping pile up into an ever-thinner, ever-fainter set of nested rings
at that radius.

**And the middle is dark.** That is the **shadow**, and it is bigger than you
would guess.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="How a black hole's silhouette comes out larger than the black hole"}
The event horizon of a non-spinning black hole is at $r_S$. Its shadow is not.

The dark patch is the set of directions on your sky along which a ray traced
backward ends on the horizon rather than escaping to infinity. Because the
geometry bends rays *inward*, a ray that would have missed the hole in flat
space can still be captured — so the hole intercepts a larger patch of sky than
its own size. Doing the null-geodesic calculation gives a shadow of radius

$$
r_{\mathrm{shadow}} = \frac{\sqrt{27}}{2}\,r_S \approx 2.60\,r_S ,
$$ {#eq-shadow}

so the shadow's **diameter** is $\sqrt{27}\,r_S \approx 5.20\,r_S$, against a
horizon diameter of $2\,r_S$. The silhouette is **2.6 times the size of the
thing casting it.**

Note that this is a bigger radius than the photon sphere at $1.5\,r_S$, and
that is not a contradiction. The photon sphere is where the orbiting light
physically is; the shadow edge is where it *appears* to be after its own light
has climbed out through the same curvature.

A spinning black hole's shadow is smaller and not quite circular, but not by
much — even at maximal spin the departure from @eq-shadow is at the few-percent
level, which is why the round-shadow prediction survives not knowing the spin.
:::

Put the shadow and the beaming together and you have the shape to look for: a
**ring of light, brighter on one side, wrapped around a dark center that is
larger than the horizon.** That is a prediction, and it is specific enough to
be wrong.

It is not wrong. The Event Horizon Telescope has now photographed two black
holes — the giant one at the center of the galaxy M87 [@eht2019m87] and
Sagittarius A\* at the center of our own [@eht2022sgra] — and both of them
look like that: a lopsided ring around a dark center of very nearly the
predicted size. We will come back to those images later in the term, when we
have the accretion physics to say what the glowing gas is actually doing.

## Putting it together

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

This one is meant to be harder than the section exercises, and it needs more
than one lecture.

**Reading a photograph.** Suppose you are handed an image of an accretion disk
in which the bright side is 20 times brighter than the faint side, and you know
nothing else about the system.

a. What is $\beta\sin i$?
b. The gas cannot orbit faster than $\beta = 0.5$ if it is outside the
   innermost stable circular orbit of a non-spinning black hole. Use that to
   put a lower bound on the inclination $i$.
c. Now suppose a spectrum of the same disk shows the two sides separated by
   a wavelength ratio of 1.4. Is that consistent with the brightness ratio
   you were given? Show your reasoning, and say what it would mean if it
   were not.

::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answers"}
a. From @eq-ratio, the color ratio is $20^{1/4} = 2.115$, so
   $\beta\sin i = (2.115 - 1)/(2.115 + 1) = 0.358$.
b. If $\beta \le 0.5$ then $\sin i \ge 0.358/0.5 = 0.716$, so
   $i \ge 45.7^{\circ}$. The disk cannot be close to face-on.
c. Not consistent. @eq-fourthpower says the brightness ratio is the fourth
   power of the color ratio, and $1.4^{4} = 3.8$, not 20. Something is
   wrong: either the two measurements are of different regions of the disk,
   or the brightness difference is not purely kinematic — a real disk is
   also hotter on the inside, and gravitational redshift is acting on top of
   everything. The point of the exercise is that the two measurements are
   *not* independent, so disagreement is informative.
:::
:::

## Summary

- **Light is a wave and a particle at once**, and the two descriptions are
  locked together: $c = \lambda\nu$ and $E = h\nu$. Short wavelength means high
  frequency means energetic photon. Visible light is a very thin slice of the
  electromagnetic spectrum, and both black hole images in this lecture were
  taken in the radio.
- **The relativistic Doppler shift**,
  $\lambda^{\prime} = \lambda(1 + v_r/c)\gamma$, has two pieces: an ordinary
  term that depends on direction and a time-dilation term that does not.
- **Motion changes brightness far more than it changes color.** The Doppler
  factor enters the observed flux four times over — once for photon energy,
  once for arrival rate, twice for the forward sweeping of the beam — so
  $F \propto \mathcal{D}^4$, and the brightness ratio across a disk is the
  **fourth power** of the wavelength ratio.
- Gas at the innermost stable circular orbit moves at **exactly half the speed
  of light**, whatever the mass, so the inner disk of a black hole really is
  tens of times brighter on one side than the other.
- **A black hole's silhouette is larger than the black hole**:
  $\sqrt{27}\,r_S/2$ in radius, or 2.6 times the horizon, because the geometry
  bends into the hole rays that would have missed it.
- Put those together and a black hole should look like **a lopsided ring of
  light around a dark center larger than the horizon** — which is what the two
  black holes that have actually been photographed look like. We return to
  those images later in the term.
- Next time we start asking not what the gas near a black hole *looks* like but
  **how much energy it gives up on the way in**, which turns out to be the most
  efficient process in the universe.
